title: Nvidia and Big Tech Propel US Market Higher as Apple and Wall Street Stocks Slip
body:
A rally in a handful of heavyweight technology names pushed the S&P 500 higher on Tuesday, offsetting a slide in Apple shares and a broadly mixed day on Wall Street. The benchmark index climbed 0.4 percent to finish at 5,419.21, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.2 percent and the Nasdaq Composite inched up 0.1 percent. The surge was led by Nvidia, whose shares surged more than 5 percent after the chipmaker posted a better‑than‑expected earnings report, and by a modest rebound in Microsoft and Alphabet, which together added enough momentum to lift the market despite the broader weakness.

Apple, the world’s most valuable public company, fell 1.7 percent after the iPhone 15 series failed to meet analysts’ sales forecasts in the latest quarter. The disappointing numbers sparked concerns that demand for premium smartphones may be softening as consumers stretch budgets amid lingering inflation pressures. The decline in Apple weighed on the technology‑heavy S&P 500, but the impact was largely neutralized by the outperformance of other mega‑caps that dominate the index’s weighting.

Nvidia’s earnings beat was the day’s headline. The graphics‑processor giant posted revenue of $8.1 billion, up 262 percent year‑over‑year, driven by explosive growth in artificial‑intelligence workloads and data‑center demand. CEO Jensen Huang highlighted a “record‑breaking” quarter and forecast continued double‑digit growth for the next twelve months. The bullish outlook sent Nvidia’s stock soaring, adding roughly 200 points to the S&P 500’s gain. Analysts noted that while Nvidia’s valuation remains lofty, its dominance in the AI chip market gives it a rare growth engine that can lift the broader market when other sectors lag.

Meanwhile, Microsoft and Alphabet each posted modest earnings surprises that helped steady the Nasdaq’s otherwise tepid performance. Microsoft’s cloud revenue grew 21 percent, reinforcing its position as a key beneficiary of enterprise digital transformation, while Alphabet’s advertising business showed resilience despite a slowdown in global ad spend. Both companies posted earnings per share that topped Wall Street expectations, prompting investors to rotate into these “safe‑haven” tech stocks as Apple’s dip raised caution flags.

The broader market, however, showed signs of unevenness. Energy stocks fell as oil prices retreated modestly, while financials were mixed, with regional banks gaining on the back of improved deposit flows but large banks slipping amid concerns over higher borrowing costs. Consumer discretionary also lagged, reflecting lingering uncertainty about the pace of economic recovery. The Dow’s decline was anchored by a drop in industrials such as Caterpillar and United Technologies, which were pressured by weaker manufacturing data released earlier in the week.

Investors appear to be navigating a delicate balance between optimism for AI‑driven growth and wariness over macro‑economic headwinds. The Federal Reserve’s recent decision to keep interest rates unchanged, coupled with signals that further hikes may be on the table, continues to shape sentiment. While the tech rally offers a short‑term boost, analysts caution that a sustained market advance will require broader participation beyond a handful of mega‑caps.

Looking ahead, market participants will be watching the upcoming earnings season closely, especially for mid‑cap technology firms and consumer‑goods companies that could either reinforce the AI‑centric narrative or expose vulnerabilities in demand. The trajectory of oil prices, the pace of Fed policy adjustments, and any fresh data on consumer spending will also be pivotal. If the tech giants can maintain their growth momentum while the rest of the economy steadies, the S&P 500 could see further incremental gains; however, a resurgence in inflation concerns or a sharper-than‑expected slowdown in consumer confidence could quickly reverse the modest upside seen this week.
